script_data.title: The Wrong Turn That Broke the World
script_data.description: A simple navigational error in Sarajevo sparked a global catastrophe that reshaped the entire 20th century.
script_data.script:
Sarajevo, June 28, 1914. The air was buzzing with an odd mix of celebratory fanfare and underlying tension. Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to the Austro-Hungarian throne, was visiting the Bosnian capital with his beloved wife, Sophie, on their 14th wedding anniversary. Their motorcade, a procession of open-topped Gräf & Stift cars, moved slowly through the sun-drenched streets, lined with curious onlookers and security forces.

Earlier that morning, a dark shadow had fallen. A bomb, thrown by a young Bosnian Serb nationalist named Nedeljko Čabrinović, had bounced off the Archduke’s car and exploded under a following vehicle, injuring several officers. Shaken but resolute, Franz Ferdinand insisted on continuing his official program, but with a crucial change of heart: he would first visit the injured officers in the hospital, a move of unexpected empathy.

This humanitarian impulse led to a fateful decision to alter the pre-planned route. The motorcade was supposed to continue along the Appel Quay, a direct route. However, due to confusion and a lack of clear communication to the lead driver, Leopold Lojka, he unknowingly turned right off the Appel Quay onto Franz Josef Street—a street not on the revised itinerary. Military Governor Oskar Potiorek, realizing the error, shouted at the driver to reverse.

It was a simple, accidental wrong turn, a navigational error of mere seconds, but one that demanded the Archduke’s car come to a complete stop directly in front of a sandwich shop. By a cosmic coincidence of the highest order, this was precisely where a dejected Gavrilo Princip, another nationalist conspirator, stood. Having given up hope after the first attempt failed, Princip found himself staring directly at his target, stationary and vulnerable, at an unimaginable range.

Without hesitation, Princip seized the impossible opportunity. He drew his pistol and fired two shots at close range. One bullet struck Sophie, the other fatally wounded Franz Ferdinand. Chaos erupted, but the damage was done. This single, accidental wrong turn, born from miscommunication and an Archduke's humanitarian impulse, became the spark. It ignited the diplomatic powder keg of Europe, unleashing a chain reaction that plunged the world into the Great War, forever altering the map of the continent, toppling empires, and laying the groundwork for the entirety of the 20th century. A wrong turn, indeed, that changed everything.
